Wise Man and the Foolish Man
WYZ-man and the FOO-lish-man
n. phrase (parable of Matthew 7:24–27 and Luke 6:47–49; hearing and obeying Christ versus hearing and neglecting Him)
Wise from Old English wīs (learned, sagacious, having knowledge that governs action); foolish from Old English fōl (foolish, senseless), from Latin follis (empty bellows, windbag). In biblical usage, wisdom and folly are not primarily intellectual categories but ethical and relational ones: the wise man in Proverbs fears God and walks in His ways; the fool says in his heart “there is no God” (Psalm 14:1) and lives without reference to divine authority. Jesus' closing parable of the Sermon on the Mount applies these categories to response to His own words.

Biblical Definition

The parable of the wise man and the foolish man closes the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 7:24–27) and its Lukan parallel (Luke 6:47–49), functioning as the Sermon's final demand and self-interpretation. Two builders both hear the same words; the sole distinguishing factor is whether they act on them. The wise man hears and acts and builds on rock; when the storm comes — rain, floods, winds beating on the house — the house stands because its foundation holds. The foolish man hears and does not act and builds on sand; the same storm reveals the fatal flaw: “the ruin of that house was great.” Jesus thus frames the entire Sermon as a test of what the hearer will do with what he has heard. The parable's structure is deliberately symmetric — same storm, same description of each builder, same sequence — to isolate the single variable: hearing plus doing versus hearing alone. The rock is not a good life strategy or moral wisdom but obedience to “these words of Mine” — the legislative word of the divine Son who has just spoken with authority the scribes could not match (Matt. 7:28–29). The parable therefore closes the Sermon christologically: the foundation-rock is not moral effort but submission to Christ's word. The storm is eschatological — the final judgment that tests every life's foundation. Reformed theology reads the parable in connection with the covenant-blessings-and-curses pattern of Deuteronomy 28–30: obedience to the covenant word brings life; neglect destroys.

Webster 1828 Definition

The closing parable of the Sermon on the Mount: hearing Christ's words and obeying them builds on rock and survives the eschatological storm; hearing and neglecting builds on sand and falls with great ruin. The sole distinguishing variable is obedience — the rock is not moral effort but submission to Christ's own word.

WISE MAN AND THE FOOLISH MAN, n. The concluding parable of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 7:24–27; Luke 6:47–49), in which two builders hear the same words of Christ and are distinguished solely by whether they act on them. The wise man hears and does; his house on rock survives the storm. The foolish man hears and neglects; his house on sand falls with great ruin.

The parable's function is self-interpretive: it closes the entire Sermon on the Mount and names what has been happening throughout — Jesus has been laying the foundation of a life that will survive eschatological judgment. The hearers have been given the words; the parable demands to know what they will do with them.

The rock is “these words of Mine” (Matthew 7:24) — Christ's own legislative word, not moral achievement or good theology in the abstract. The distinction between rock and sand is not between good effort and bad effort but between obedient hearing and mere hearing. This guards against the moralistic reading that makes the rock a self-built foundation of righteous works.

The storm is eschatological in its weight: in Matthew's context, the same imagery of rain, floods, and winds appears in apocalyptic literature for the final judgment. The parable does not promise that the wise man's house will never be tested; it promises that the house built on Christ's word will withstand the test that finally unmasks every false foundation.

Luke's version (6:47–49) adds the detail that the wise man “dug deep” to lay his foundation on the rock — emphasizing the costly labor of genuine obedience. Sand-building is faster and easier; rock-building requires excavation. Discipleship that costs nothing is the parable's portrait of sand.

Key Scripture

Matthew 7:24 — "Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine, and acts upon them, may be compared to a wise man, who built his house upon the rock."

Matthew 7:26 — "And everyone who hears these words of Mine, and does not act upon them, will be like a foolish man, who built his house upon the sand."

Luke 6:47 — "Everyone who comes to Me, and hears My words and acts upon them, I will show you whom he is like."

Luke 6:49 — "But the one who has heard, and has not acted accordingly, is like a man who built a house upon the ground, without any foundation — and the torrent burst against it, and immediately it collapsed. And the ruin of that house was great.”"

Modern Corruption

Liberal Protestantism reduces the parable to a general moral lesson about sincere effort versus hypocrisy, stripping its christological center (“these words of Mine”); prosperity Christianity promises that the rock-builder will be spared all storms rather than sustained through them.

expand to see more

Liberal Protestant and moralistic readings of the parable dissolve “these words of Mine” into “good values” or “sincere moral effort” and identify the rock as any ethical seriousness regardless of its Christological grounding. In this reading, the wise man is not the disciple of Christ but anyone who acts on noble principles — a reading that removes Christ from the center of the parable He told about Himself. The parable is not about builders in general; it is about hearers of “these words of Mine” specifically — the words of the one who has just taught with authority surpassing the scribes (Matt. 7:28–29). Remove the christological center and the parable becomes a self-help metaphor for intentional living.

Prosperity-gospel Christianity inverts the parable's storm-teaching: in the prosperity framework, the rock-builder is protected from adversity — health, financial stability, and blessing are promised to the obedient. The parable, however, says nothing about the rock-builder being spared the storm; it says his house will survive it. Both builders face the same storm, the same rain, the same floods. The distinction is not between those who escape testing and those who face it but between those whose foundation holds and those whose foundation fails. The cross is the rock-builder's promised experience before the resurrection is theirs.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The wise-man-foolish-man parable draws on Proverbs' wisdom-vs.-folly contrast, the Deuteronomic covenant-blessings-and-curses pattern, the Psalter's two-ways motif (Psalm 1), and the house-building metaphor of the Wisdom literature — all crystallized in the closing demand of the Sermon on the Mount.

expand to see more

Psalm 1 (two-ways motif) — the blessed man who meditates on the law and the wicked man who does not; the righteous man is like a tree planted by water (unshaken); the wicked are like chaff the wind drives away; the two-ways contrast structures the parable's two-builder symmetry.

Proverbs 24:3–4 (house built by wisdom) — “By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established”; the Wisdom tradition's house-building metaphor is the immediate background for Jesus' parable, with wisdom now identified as hearing and obeying Christ's word.

Deuteronomy 28–30 (covenant blessings and curses) — the Mosaic covenant's two-outcome structure: obedience to the covenant word brings life and blessing; disobedience brings curse and destruction; the parable applies the same pattern to response to Christ's covenant word.

Ezekiel 13:10–16 (wall daubed with whitewash) — the false prophet who built the wall and daubed it with whitewash (sand-foundation ministry) that collapses in the storm of divine judgment; Ezekiel's image is the direct prophetic precursor to Jesus' parable.

Matthew 7:28–29 (authority response) — the crowd's recognition that Jesus taught as one having authority closes the Sermon's immediate context; the rock of the parable is the word of the one who speaks with divine authority, not the word of the scribes who cited prior authorities.

Usage

"The parable's diagnostic force comes from its symmetry: both builders heard the Sermon, both presumably affirmed it as admirable, both were in the crowd on the mountain — the difference between them did not appear until the storm; profession without obedience is indistinguishable from genuine discipleship until the crisis reveals the foundation."

"Luke's detail that the wise man “dug deep” (6:48) corrects the superficial reading that the only variable is internal disposition: genuine obedience requires labor, excavation through the soft surface to the bedrock of Christ's word; quick-build discipleship that avoids the cost is sand-building even when it feels like rock."

"Preachers who conclude with the application “apply this to your life” are actually enacting the parable: the Sermon on the Mount itself ends with the demand to act — the preacher who draws the same line between hearing and doing at the end of every sermon is following Jesus' own homiletical pattern."
